proposedDescription: Citricola scale is a sap-feeding insect that can leave citrus foliage sticky with honeydew and darkened by sooty mold. Its appearance changes as it grows: young scales are flat and translucent beneath leaves, while mature females become oval, grayish bumps on twigs. Heavy populations can weaken trees and reduce fruit production. Ants, sticky leaves and black mold are useful clues, but checking the insects themselves matters because several other citrus pests leave the same signs.
identification: Look beneath leaves for flat young scales and along twigs for convex gray females, up to about 6 mm long. Brown soft scale is generally smaller and browner; identification should include life stage.
actions: Photograph both leaf and twig colonies and ask an extension specialist to confirm the scale. Preserve predators and parasitoids; management timing varies with local climate and the insect's stage.
researchNotes: UC guidance supplies life stages and regional management; the independently authored Croatian paper corroborates citrus injury. Croatian access was an abstract, not its full article.

sources.title: Citricola scale in citrus plantations in Croatia

claims: Young scales occupy leaf undersides before moving to twigs.
Mature females are gray and convex.
Heavy infestations produce honeydew, sooty mold and reduced tree vigor.

proposedDescription: Citron zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with bright yellow flowers held above a tuft of very narrow leaves. Each flower sits on a slender, upright stalk, giving the plant a light, grassy appearance between blooms. Native to parts of Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, it is also cultivated well beyond that range. A garden planting and a self-sustaining wild population are different situations, so location and evidence of seedlings are useful details when recording it.
identification: Look for linear leaves only a few millimeters wide, an underground bulb, and yellow flowers about 3–4 cm long on stalks roughly 15–25 cm tall. Confirm with flowers rather than foliage alone.
actions: Record whether plants were planted or are appearing independently nearby. Photograph flowers, leaves and the surrounding habitat; avoid discarding bulbs or seed-bearing material in natural areas.
researchNotes: Kew's independent Flora of the Cayman Islands account provides measurements; NParks documents cultivated habit and propagation. Neither source establishes a harmful invasion at every introduced locality.

proposedDescription: Citrus black spot is a fungal disease that marks citrus fruit with several kinds of blemishes, from tiny dark speckles to sunken spots with pale centers and dark borders. Severe infections can cause fruit to drop before harvest. The fungus can reproduce in infected fallen leaves, helping the disease persist around a tree. Because symptoms vary with the fruit's age and can resemble other problems, a photograph is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable confirmation.
identification: Hard-spot symptoms include small, circular, sunken lesions with gray or tan centers and dark margins. Other forms look quite different; have suspicious fruit and leaf symptoms assessed by a plant diagnostic service.
actions: Photograph suspect fruit and contact local extension or the state plant health office. Avoid moving potentially infected citrus plants, fruit or fallen material until you receive local guidance.
researchNotes: APHIS and University of Florida independently provide disease and diagnostic guidance. Description avoids the overly broad claim that lesions never affect tissue beneath the rind.

sources.title: UF IFAS: A guide to citrus disease identification

Movement of infected material can spread the disease.

proposedDescription: Despite its name, citrus blackfly belongs to the whitefly family. Adults are dark and sooty-looking, and their young form conspicuous black, spiny patches beneath leaves. Feeding removes plant sap and produces honeydew, which can support a coating of sooty mold. Citrus is an important host, though many other woody plants can carry it. Natural enemies can keep populations low, so finding a few insects does not automatically mean a tree needs treatment.
identification: Check leaf undersides for eggs laid in spirals and dark, spiny immature stages. The final immature stage has a pale waxy fringe; adults have slate-blue to blackish wings.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and photograph the underside of affected leaves. Seek identification and local advice before treatment, especially where parasitoids already suppress this pest; avoid moving infested nursery plants.
researchNotes: UF supplies detailed identification and Florida biological-control experience; EPPO adds independently sourced host and movement information. Florida control success is not presented as universal.

claims: Eggs occur in spirals beneath leaves.
Immatures are black and spiny, with wax around the pupal covering.
Parasitoids provide effective suppression in Florida.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: EPPO synthesis of international plant protection studies

proposedDescription: The name on this record needs a closer check before it can support a citrus canker profile. Xanthomonas campestris is a recognized bacterial species, while older citrus literature used the more specific name Xanthomonas campestris pv. citri for the canker pathogen now placed in Xanthomonas citri. Dropping that final pathovar name changes the meaning. Resolving the original identification will help ensure that citrus symptoms and reporting advice are attached to the right organism.
identification: The species name alone cannot identify the historical citrus-infecting pathovar. Trace the original record, diagnostic result or cited name before assigning citrus canker symptoms to this entry.
actions: Refer the naming conflict to a taxonomic or plant diagnostic reviewer. Keep the existing identifier intact and withhold a definitive citrus canker interpretation until its intended taxon is resolved.
researchNotes: Research gap: common name Citrus canker conflicts with the unspecialized species name Xanthomonas campestris. EPPO lists X. campestris pv. citri as a historical synonym, not X. campestris in its entirety.

proposedDescription: Citrus canker is caused by a citrus-infecting pathovar of Xanthomonas citri, a bacterium that attacks leaves, shoots and fruit. Its raised, corky lesions often have a yellow halo and can make fruit unsaleable; severe disease also causes leaf and fruit drop. Wind-driven rain helps bacteria reach young tissue and wounds. Nursery plants can carry infection between places, including before clear symptoms appear, making careful diagnosis and plant-movement precautions especially important.
identification: Look for raised, rough or crater-like brown lesions, often with a water-soaked edge or yellow halo. Similar-looking damage needs laboratory or plant-health confirmation.
actions: Document symptoms without transporting the plant or affected material. Contact extension or the local plant health authority for sampling instructions and applicable movement requirements.
researchNotes: The reviewed organism is Xanthomonas citri pv. citri; the database species ID is broader and remains unchanged. No claim is made that every X. citri pathovar causes citrus canker.

Moisture and wind-driven rain favor infection.

proposedDescription: Huanglongbing, often called citrus greening, is a serious citrus disease associated with the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. Infected trees may develop unevenly mottled leaves, yellow shoots and small, misshapen fruit that remain partly green. The Asian citrus psyllid carries the bacterium between trees, and infected propagation material can also spread it. Symptoms may take time to appear, so a healthy-looking tree is not proof of freedom from infection. Confirmed disease has no cure.
identification: Asymmetric yellow blotching across a leaf's midrib is a useful warning sign. Small lopsided fruit and shoot dieback add concern, but nutrient disorders and other problems can look similar; laboratory testing is needed.
actions: Photograph suspicious foliage and fruit and contact the local plant health office. Avoid moving citrus plants, cuttings or suspect green waste until you have appropriate guidance.
researchNotes: Uses the accepted provisional bacterial prefix Candidatus while preserving the database ID. APHIS and UC IPM independently describe transmission, diagnostic uncertainty and lack of curative treatment.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Citrus greening and Asian citrus psyllid

Infected trees may lack visible symptoms and there is no cure.

proposedDescription: Citrus leafminer leaves a delicate silver trail as its larvae tunnel just beneath the surface of new citrus leaves. The narrow, winding mine often contains a dark line of waste, and damaged leaves may curl around the developing insect. Young trees can lose valuable new growth, while established trees usually tolerate the injury. Feeding wounds can also make citrus canker infection easier where that disease occurs. The tiny adult moth is much less noticeable than its handiwork.
identification: Look for winding mines with a central dark line on tender leaves and a curled leaf edge where pupation occurs. Adults are tiny silvery moths with dark marks near the wing tips.
actions: Keep damaged leaves that are still functioning, and avoid unnecessary pruning or excessive fertilization that prompts repeated flushes of tender growth. Preserve parasitoids and seek local advice if young trees are badly affected.
researchNotes: UF provides life cycle and canker relationship; UC IPM independently addresses tolerance, identification and garden or orchard management.

claims: Larvae mine young citrus leaves.
Feeding injury can facilitate citrus canker infection.
Adults are very small moths.
Mines contain a central frass line and leaves may curl.
Mature trees usually tolerate injury.

proposedDescription: Citrus mealybug looks like a small moving fleck of white cotton, often tucked into a leaf joint, fruit cluster or other sheltered spot. Beneath its waxy coating is an oval sap-feeding insect with short filaments around the body. It attacks many ornamentals as well as citrus, including plants grown indoors. Colonies can weaken growth and leave sticky honeydew that encourages sooty mold. New plants deserve a close inspection because small colonies are easy to overlook.
identification: Females have white wax, a faint grayish stripe along the back and short marginal filaments, with the rear pair slightly longer. Look for cottony egg sacs and hidden colonies; related mealybugs can require expert examination.
actions: Inspect and isolate newly acquired houseplants when insects are found. Remove small accessible colonies, then recheck crevices over several weeks; obtain pest-specific advice for persistent or extensive infestations.
researchNotes: UF provides host range and morphology; NC State's separately authored extension account provides inspection and repeated follow-up guidance.

claims: Females are oval, wax-covered insects with short marginal filaments.
The insect has a broad host range.
Colonies produce honeydew and hide in protected plant sites.
Citrus mealybug infests ornamental houseplants.
Minor colonies can be removed individually.
Repeated observation is needed after removal.

proposedDescription: Citrus rust mite is so small that the damage usually catches your eye before the animal does. Feeding on rind cells can leave oranges rusty brown and lemons silvery, changing the fruit's appearance. These pale, wedge-shaped mites also feed on leaves and green stems. In home gardens, light injury is often mainly cosmetic, but heavier infestations can matter in commercial production and may contribute to fruit drop. The similar pink citrus rust mite is a different species.
identification: A strong hand lens is needed: adults are less than about 0.25 mm long, pale yellow to brownish and wedge-shaped, with four legs near the front. Confirm the mite rather than relying on rind color alone.
actions: Inspect affected fruit with magnification and assess the amount of injury before considering treatment. Garden fruit with superficial blemishes may not need intervention; growers should use local monitoring thresholds.
researchNotes: UC's home-garden account and UF's commercial citrus review describe different levels of consequence; the draft retains that distinction and separates the pink rust mite.

proposedDescription: This clam worm lives out of sight in the mud of brackish estuaries, where its segmented body moves through a burrow. Native to the northwestern Pacific, Hediste diadroma has also been identified in estuaries on North America's Pacific coast. It gathers food from sediment and can filter suspended particles through a mucus net. Its resemblance to native worms makes casual sightings difficult to interpret, and the ecological effects of its introduction remain uncertain.
identification: A tapered, many-segmented worm with bristled side appendages and four eyes is consistent with this group, but not enough for species identification. Specialists use fine anatomical features and sometimes molecular evidence to separate similar Hediste.
actions: Record the location and habitat without transferring worms or sediment between sites. Ask a marine invertebrate specialist to assess a suspected record; photographs alone may not resolve the species.
researchNotes: Smithsonian supplies invasion history, morphology and explicit impact uncertainty. Independent laboratory feeding observations were read as the published J-STAGE abstract; no experiment is proposed here.

proposedDescription: Clammy goosefoot is a low, spreading herb whose small leaves and tiny flower clusters are easy to miss underfoot. Fine glandular hairs give it an aromatic, somewhat sticky character. The flowers sit close to the stems in the leaf axils, later producing minute dark seeds. Native to Australia, it has become established in other regions, often around disturbed or cultivated ground. Its modest appearance means close-up details are more useful than a distant photograph.
identification: Look for prostrate or partly ascending stems, small oval leaves with wavy or toothed margins, glandular hairs and dense, tiny whitish flower clusters where leaves meet stems. Confirm against other small goosefoots.
actions: Photograph the leaf margins, flower clusters and growth habit. Ask a local herbarium or extension service to confirm uncertain plants before deciding whether removal is warranted.
researchNotes: Independent Flora of NSW and Flora of Tropical East Africa descriptions support morphology and contrasting native versus introduced contexts. No broad ecological impact is established by these sources.

proposedDescription: Clasping heliotrope forms low, sprawling patches topped with curved clusters of blue-purple to pink flowers, each with a small yellow center. Its hairy, wavy-edged leaves sit close to the stems. This South American perennial can persist through a deep root system and regrow after its shoots die back. In introduced pasture settings it can compete with useful vegetation, and its toxicity to livestock makes a confirmed identification especially important around grazing land.
identification: Check for hairy, mostly stalkless leaves that partly clasp the stem and coiled flower clusters with blooms arranged along one side in two rows. It is often called blue heliotrope.
actions: Keep livestock away from suspected patches until a local agricultural adviser confirms the plant and assesses the situation. Record patch size and flowering details; obtain locally appropriate management advice.
researchNotes: NSW WeedWise supplies field characters and Australian pasture effects; USDA GRIN independently documents South American origin and toxicity literature. No universal legal status or treatment prescription is implied.

claims: Low perennial with hairy leaves and blue-purple flowers with yellow centers.

proposedDescription: Clasping pepperweed has an unusual contrast between its leaves: the lower ones are finely divided, while the upper ones are broad and wrap closely around the stem. Small yellow flowers appear above them, followed by little rounded seed pods. This short-lived mustard comes from Eurasia and is introduced in North America, where it often grows on dry, disturbed ground. Seeing both the lower foliage and the flowering stem makes identification much easier.
identification: Look for deeply dissected lower leaves, strongly clasping rounded upper leaves, four small yellow petals and flattened, roughly oval fruits about 4 mm long. Other clasping mustards need comparison.
actions: Include upper and lower leaves, flowers and mature pods in photographs. Consult a local flora or extension service if the plant cannot be distinguished from similar mustards.
researchNotes: Burke Herbarium's authored field account supplies morphology and habitat; Kew's independent range synthesis corroborates Eurasian origin and annual or biennial life history. Neither is used to infer local absence.

claims: Lower leaves are divided and upper leaves strongly clasp the stem.

proposedDescription: Claspleaf pennycress is a small annual mustard with pale green foliage, tiny white flowers and flattened seed pods with a noticeable notch at the tip. Upper leaves clasp the stem, while lower leaves form a loose rosette. It occurs in dry, often lime-rich soils and can grow among crops and orchard vegetation. Botanical references may call it Microthlaspi perfoliatum, Thlaspi perfoliatum or Noccaea perfoliata, so matching the plant's features is more useful than relying on one name alone.
identification: Look for a low upright plant, oval to oblong clasping stem leaves, small white flowers and broadly winged, notched pods. Fruit shape helps distinguish it from other small spring mustards.
actions: Photograph mature pods beside a scale along with the upper leaf bases. Ask a local herbarium or extension specialist to resolve uncertain identification before treating it as a weed of concern.
researchNotes: Kew accepts Noccaea perfoliata and places Microthlaspi perfoliatum in synonymy; database ID retained. INRA's independently authored botanical and crop-habitat account supplies the substantive field description; Kew adds native range and annual habit.

proposedDescription: Cotton leaf curl Gezira virus is a plant virus associated with leaf-curl disease in cotton and other members of the mallow family, including okra. Affected leaves may curl and develop thickened veins, but those changes are not unique to this virus. Reports from ornamental mallows have added another layer of uncertainty because findings in one host do not establish the same disease behavior in another. Reliable identification depends on a professional plant-health diagnosis.
identification: Curled leaves and thickened veins are warning signs, not a species-level diagnosis. Other viruses, pests and growing conditions can cause similar-looking damage.
actions: Document the host plant and visible symptoms and consult an extension plant pathologist or official plant-health service. Let qualified professionals determine whether further diagnostic assessment is appropriate.
researchNotes: NVWA's 2025 risk-assessment summary explicitly notes uncertainty about ornamental-mallow isolates; the independent UAE okra disease report was read as a PubMed abstract. No current regional absence or experimental procedure is inferred.

proposedDescription: Climbing false buckwheat is an annual vine that threads its way through nearby vegetation with slender, twining stems. Its leaves are triangular to heart-shaped, and the small flowers are much less showy than those of a morning glory. As fruits develop, the surrounding flower parts form pale wings. Native across temperate Eurasia, it also occurs in disturbed North American habitats. It closely resembles native climbing false buckwheats, making mature fruit an important part of a useful record.
identification: Examine alternate, unlobed leaves and mature fruiting flower parts. In this species the latter are commonly about 4.2–6.5 mm long and narrow abruptly near the base; compare carefully with Fallopia scandens.
actions: Photograph ripe fruiting structures and leaf bases, not just the climbing habit. Seek a botanist's confirmation before removing a vine that could be a native lookalike.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust supplies detailed comparison with F. scandens; Kew independently establishes temperate Eurasian native range. The broad range follows Kew rather than the narrower informal origin wording in Go Botany.

proposedDescription: Climbing nightshade scrambles through shrubs and fences, especially in moist places. Its purple flowers have petals that curve backward around a bright yellow center, and its berries ripen through several colors before turning glossy red. This perennial vine is native to Eurasia and has become established in North America, where it can spread through underground stems as well as seed. The attractive berries are not edible; all parts of the plant are toxic to people and domestic animals.
identification: Look for clusters of purple, backward-curving petals surrounding a yellow cone, red ripe berries and alternate leaves that may have two small basal lobes. It is also called bittersweet nightshade.
actions: Keep children and pets from eating berries and wear gloves when handling the plant. Ask local extension for identification or management advice, particularly around waterways or mixed native vegetation.
researchNotes: Independent Utah State and NC State extension accounts agree on perennial habit, characteristic flowers, underground stems and toxicity. No ingestion or medicinal use is suggested.

proposedDescription: Climbing fig can turn a wall into a dense covering of small, heart-shaped leaves. This woody evergreen vine, native to eastern Asia, attaches itself with short roots along its young stems. As it matures, it develops thicker branches with much larger, leathery leaves and may produce pear-shaped figs. That change can make the adult plant look surprisingly different from its familiar juvenile form. Its strong attachment to surfaces also deserves consideration wherever it is planted near buildings.
identification: Young climbing shoots have small heart-shaped leaves and attaching roots; mature projecting branches carry larger oval leaves and sometimes green-to-purple, pear-shaped figs.
actions: Keep established garden vines within their intended space and assess the surface before allowing them to climb a building. Photograph both juvenile and mature shoots when requesting identification.
researchNotes: NC State independently explains juvenile versus adult foliage and attachment; NParks supports woody habit, Asian origin and pruning context. Conflicting edibility remarks are deliberately omitted.

claims: Evergreen woody climber attaches by short roots.

proposedDescription: Clinging jellyfish are small enough to overlook among seagrass and seaweed. Their transparent bells carry a conspicuous orange-brown cross, and sticky pads on the tentacles help them hold onto submerged vegetation. They occur in sheltered coastal waters such as bays, estuaries and ponds, rather than behaving like large jellies drifting conspicuously offshore. Contact can cause a painful sting, with reactions varying between people and populations. A clear photograph taken without touching the animal is the safest useful observation.
identification: Look for a transparent bell a few centimeters across, a colored cross and numerous fine tentacles associated with submerged plants. Small size and similar jellyfish make expert confirmation valuable.
actions: Avoid touching or collecting suspected animals. Follow local beach or marine-agency advice and report a sighting with its location and a photograph if one can be taken safely.
researchNotes: Independent Rhode Island field confirmation and Swedish marine-agency account agree on appearance, vegetation association and variable sting severity. Historical sightings are not used as a current distribution map; medical treatment instructions are omitted.

proposedDescription: Clover dodder makes a fine tangle of yellowish, red or purple threads over other plants, with tiny rounded clusters of flowers along its stems. It draws nourishment directly from its hosts, which include clovers, heather and gorse, rather than supporting itself with ordinary green leaves. Its role depends on the setting: it can trouble agricultural crops, yet it is also a native part of European heathland. The identity of both the dodder and its host helps explain a sighting.
identification: Look for slender twining stems, leaves reduced to minute scales and tightly packed clusters of tiny five-parted flowers. Flower details are needed to separate it from other dodders.
actions: Photograph the flowers, threads and host plant. Seek local botanical or agricultural advice before removal, particularly in native heathland or conservation areas.
researchNotes: Kew's own species profile covers parasitic habit, hosts and contrasting agricultural/conservation context. The independent Flora of NSW account corroborates morphology and introduced habitat; no blanket invasive label is applied.

proposedDescription: The clover weevil, also called clover root curculio, is a small mottled brown beetle associated with clover and alfalfa. Adults nibble small semicircular notches along leaf edges, but the more serious injury happens underground. Pale larvae feed on roots and can leave scars or deep gouges that weaken plants. A thinning patch of forage may therefore reflect damage that is not visible above ground, although disease and poor nutrition can produce similar symptoms.
identification: Adults are about 4 mm long, mottled brown with pale markings and fine raised hairs. Larvae are white grubs with pale brown heads. Leaf notches and root scars are clues, not proof of the species.
actions: Have an agricultural adviser assess declining forage and identify any insects found. Record whether damage involves leaf margins, roots or both rather than assuming every weakened patch has the same cause.
researchNotes: Independent UC and Utah State accounts describe adult versus larval injury. Geographic differences and limited California impact data are retained by avoiding universal severity or seasonal claims.

proposedDescription: Cotton leafroll dwarf virus can be associated with curled or puckered leaves, distorted new growth and changes in the way cotton plants develop. Some affected plants become stunted, while others show elongated shoots with poor boll production. Symptoms vary with the cotton variety, growing conditions and the stage at which disease develops; some infected plants show little obvious change. Similar leaf distortion can result from insects or herbicide injury, so appearance alone cannot establish the diagnosis.
identification: Possible signs include cupped or crinkled young leaves, reddish veins and unusual shoot growth. These signs overlap with other cotton disorders and require professional diagnostic assessment.
actions: Document symptoms and their pattern across the field and contact an extension cotton specialist or plant pathologist. Treat visual suspicion as a reason to investigate, not a confirmed virus record.
researchNotes: Separately authored Mississippi State and Alabama Extension accounts include their own regional observations. The draft avoids transferring severe losses from one region or strain to all infections, and contains no laboratory procedures.

proposedDescription: Clubed begonia forms a soft mound of fleshy stems and glossy green leaves, with small white or pink flowers held above the foliage. The leaves have a wavy, finely toothed edge, and the seed capsules are unevenly winged. Native to South America, this begonia is grown ornamentally and has escaped cultivation in some warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States. Its many garden relatives and hybrids make a flowering, fruiting specimen more informative than a familiar garden name.
identification: Look for succulent stems, broadly heart-shaped leaves with scalloped or toothed margins, white-to-pink flowers and three-winged capsules. Do not assume every bedding plant sold as wax begonia is this species.
actions: Record whether plants are cultivated or growing independently beyond a garden. Photograph flowers and capsules, and ask a local botanist or extension service to distinguish species from cultivated hybrids.
researchNotes: UF's species account supports Florida escape context and capsule morphology; NParks independently provides species-level foliage and flower details. Characteristics of the entire wax-begonia hybrid group are not assigned to this taxon.

Plants produce many tiny seeds.
South American succulent herb.
Leaves have wavy, toothed margins.
Flowers are pink or white tinged with rose-pink.

proposedDescription: Cluster mallow carries small pale flowers close to the stem, tucked into tight groups where the leaf stalks join it. Its broad, rounded leaves usually have shallow lobes and scalloped edges, giving a leafy plant a much larger presence than its flowers suggest. It has a long history of cultivation and also grows in fields, roadsides and disturbed ground. Several mallows look similar, and published records themselves sometimes reflect misidentification, so mature fruit is especially valuable for checking a sighting.
identification: Look for rounded, shallowly five- to seven-lobed leaves and nearly stalkless flower clusters in the leaf axils. The small wheel-like fruit separates into segments whose surface details help distinguish similar mallows.
actions: Photograph open flowers and mature fruit as well as the whole plant. Request a botanical identification if the fruit characters are unclear; a broad leaf photograph alone is often insufficient.
researchNotes: Independent Flora of Tropical East Africa and Flora Novae Angliae accounts both emphasize confusion among weedy mallows. Avoids uncertain fruit-edge measurements and does not repeat a potentially flawed regional range as definitive.

sources.title: Kew: Malva verticillata, Flora of Tropical East Africa account

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of Tropical East Africa, Verdcourt and Mwachala
claims: Broad rounded leaves have shallow lobes.
Flowers form dense axillary clusters.
Similar weedy Malva specimens can be difficult to identify.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: Flowers are sessile or nearly so in axillary clusters.
Mature fruit segment characters distinguish similar mallows.
Some distribution records may reflect misidentification.

proposedDescription: Clustered clover is a small annual that spreads low over the ground or lifts its stems slightly above surrounding vegetation. Its pink to purplish flowers gather in tight, rounded heads nestled directly against the stem at the leaf joints. Each leaf has the familiar three leaflets, but the almost stalkless flower heads help distinguish it from more familiar garden and pasture clovers. Native around Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, it has also become naturalized elsewhere.
identification: Look for hairless, prostrate or ascending stems, three small finely toothed leaflets and compact globular flower heads in the leaf axils. Heads are essentially stalkless, unlike those of many other clovers.
actions: Photograph the attachment of a flower head to the stem and the leaflet edges. Consult a local flora or extension service when several small clovers occur together.
researchNotes: Independent New Zealand and NSW floras agree on annual habit and head placement. Their reported flower lengths differ, so the draft uses shared qualitative characters rather than forcing a single measurement.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Trifolium glomeratum

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of New Zealand / Manaaki Whenua
claims: Annual with prostrate or ascending stems that do not root at nodes.
Globular axillary heads are sessile or very shortly stalked.
Flowers are pink to purplish.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney / Flora of NSW
claims: Hairless annual with three finely toothed leaflets.
Compact flower heads sit in leaf axils.
Native to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, naturalized in NSW.

proposedDescription: Clustered dock is a slender perennial with branching upright stems and small flowers arranged in separated whorls. Many of those clusters have a little leaf beneath them, giving the flowering stem a more leafy appearance than some other docks. It grows in damp places as well as cultivated and pasture ground, and has been introduced well beyond its native Old World range. The modest flowers are easy to overlook, but the mature fruit coverings provide useful identification details.
identification: Check for spaced flower or fruit clusters, leafy bracts beneath many whorls and three small, smooth-edged fruit valves, each with a prominent swollen grain. Mature fruit is needed to separate similar docks.
actions: Include the lower leaves and close-up mature fruit in a record. Ask a botanist or extension service to check difficult plants, especially where several dock species or hybrids occur.
researchNotes: Independent Flora of NSW and Flora of Iraq accounts support flowering structure, fruit characters and habitat. Neither generalized weed status nor uncertain New England records are treated as confirmed local invasion.

sources.title: Kew: Rumex conglomeratus, Flora of Iraq account

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney / Flora of NSW
claims: Slender perennial with separated, often leafy flower whorls.
Fruiting valves bear large swellings.
Occurs as a weed in cultivation and pasture.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of Iraq, Ghazanfar and Edmondson 2016
claims: Branched perennial with clustered flowers and leafy bracts.
Each entire fruit valve bears a large tubercle.
Habitats include shaded damp places and stream banks; hybrids occur.

proposedDescription: Coastal burnweed is an upright, short-lived herb with narrow, regularly toothed leaves and clusters of small cylindrical flower heads. Unlike a showy daisy, its heads lack a ring of spreading ray petals. Botanists now commonly treat this plant as Senecio minimus, while Erechtites minimus remains a name used in older records. It occurs naturally in Australia and New Zealand, including moist forest settings, so its presence there should not automatically be interpreted as an alien invasion.
identification: Look for narrow stem leaves with toothed bases that clasp the stem, small cylindrical heads and no showy ray flowers. Closely related Senecio species can require examination of head bracts and mature fruits.
actions: Photograph leaf bases, flower heads and the whole plant. Confirm the identification and local native status with a herbarium before considering management.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand explicitly links Erechtites minimus to Senecio minimus; independent Flora of NSW supplies morphology and wet-forest context. Database ID retained. Native occurrence is distinguished from introduced occurrence elsewhere.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Senecio minimus

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of New Zealand / Manaaki Whenua
claims: Erechtites minimus is a synonym of Senecio minimus.
Erect annual or short-lived perennial with toothed clasping leaves and no ray florets.
The species belongs to New Zealand's indigenous flora.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney / Flora of NSW
claims: Erect herb with narrow, regularly toothed, stem-clasping leaves.
Small cylindrical heads occur in branched clusters.
Native Australian populations colonize wet forest settings.

proposedDescription: Coastal wattle is a dense shrub or small tree with narrow, leathery leaf-like structures and round golden flower heads. Its most striking feature appears when the pods open: each dark seed is surrounded by a fleshy orange to scarlet loop. Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia, it has been planted elsewhere for shelter and dune stabilization. Outside its native range it can become invasive; South African conservation assessments identify it as a threat to sensitive coastal plant habitat.
identification: Look for narrow phyllodes with three or four main veins, spherical yellow flower heads and thick pods that twist after opening. The conspicuous red-orange structure around each dark seed is especially useful.
actions: Record pods, seeds and foliage when seeking confirmation. Check local native status and land-management guidance before planting or removing coastal wattles, particularly in dune or conservation areas.
researchNotes: VicFlora supplies independent morphology and native Australian range. SANBI's original Erica occulta assessment documents a specific conservation threat from A. cyclops, not a global impact estimate or current legal category.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria / Flora of Victoria
claims: Dense shrub or small tree with narrow multi-veined phyllodes and golden globular flower heads.
Seeds have fleshy orange-to-scarlet surrounding structures.
Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: South African National Biodiversity Institute, Turner and Oliver assessment
claims: Acacia cyclops infestations are identified as a threat to Erica occulta habitat on the southern Agulhas Plain.
Cleared invasive vegetation requires ongoing management at the assessed locality.

proposedDescription: Coatbuttons carries little daisy-like heads on long, wiry stalks above a low tangle of hairy stems and coarsely toothed leaves. A yellow center is bordered by just a few short white, cream or pale yellow rays, giving each head its button-like appearance. The plant is native to tropical America and is now widespread in warm regions elsewhere. It readily occupies bare and disturbed soil, where sprawling stems can form small patches between taller plants.
identification: Look for rough-hairy, toothed leaves, long solitary flower stalks and a small yellow-centered head with only a few short, often three-toothed pale rays. Mature fruits carry feathery bristles.
actions: Photograph the flower head from above and the leafy stems below it. Confirm uncertain plants with a local flora or extension service and note whether the patch is in disturbed ground or natural vegetation.
researchNotes: Kew-hosted tropical floras provide detailed morphology and native range; the Indian Institute of Science herbarium independently documents abundant occurrence on disturbed soil in India. No medicinal efficacy or universal invasive impact is asserted.

sources.title: Kew: Tridax procumbens, tropical flora descriptions
Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB: Tridax procumbens

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of the Cayman Islands and Flora of Tropical East Africa
claims: Hairy sprawling plant with coarsely toothed leaves.
Long-stalked heads have yellow disc florets and a few short pale rays.
Native to tropical America and introduced widely in the Old World tropics.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB, Indian regional floras
claims: The plant is widespread and abundant where soil is disturbed.
Indian records document occurrence across multiple regions outside its native American range.

proposedDescription: Cochineal cactus grows into a branching shrub or small tree, with flattened green pads and slender scarlet flowers. Despite its often nearly spineless appearance, the pads can carry tiny irritating bristles. Native to Mexico, it has been planted widely in warm regions and sometimes grows beyond cultivation. It also has a long history as a host for insects used to produce cochineal dye. Its presence in a garden is different from an established wild population, so records need that context.
identification: Look for elongated, flattened green pads and red flowers with conspicuously projecting stamens. Other prickly pears can look similar; photograph flowers and the whole plant.
actions: Avoid bare-handed handling. If a plant is spreading outside cultivation, photograph it and ask a local plant specialist to confirm its identity before removal.
researchNotes: Kew accepts Opuntia cochenillifera; Nopalea cochenillifera remains the queue identifier. The reviewed sources support cultivation and naturalization, not a blanket claim of ecological harm throughout the United States.

sources.title: Indian Institute of Science: Opuntia cochenillifera

claims: Mexican origin, pad and flower morphology, cultivation and cochineal history.
Independent regional flora documents its widespread occurrence outside the Americas.
Independent description of branching pads, red flowers and easy rooting of pads.

proposedDescription: Cockroach berry is a prickly, short-lived member of the nightshade family, with broad leaves, white star-shaped flowers, and round fruits that turn orange-red. It grows in disturbed ground in warm, moist regions, including places outside its native tropical American range. The bright fruit can make it conspicuous along a roadside or neglected patch, but appearance alone is not a safe guide to edibility. Similar prickly nightshades have often been confused with it, making careful identification especially useful.
identification: Check for yellowish prickles, broad sometimes lobed leaves, small clusters of white flowers, and orange-scarlet berries. Detailed fruit and seed features help specialists separate related species.
actions: Photograph the leaves, prickles, flowers, and fruit without tasting them. Wear gloves if handling a confirmed plant, and seek local advice before controlling a larger patch.
researchNotes: PlantNET's older treatment uses Solanum aculeatissimum as a synonym; Kew distinguishes the names. Draft uses shared morphological evidence and keeps the broader tropical-American origin instead of conflicting narrower origins.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Solanum capsicoides

claims: Tropical American origin and confusion with other prickly nightshades.
Prickles, white flowers, orange-scarlet berries, and disturbed moist habitats.

proposedDescription: Cockspur coral tree brings clusters of vivid red, pea-shaped flowers to a branching shrub or small tree. Its leaves are divided into three leaflets, and the branches carry prickles. Native to South America, it is grown as an ornamental in warmer regions and has been introduced well beyond its original range.
identification: Look for three-part leaves, prickly branches, and elongated red flowers held in clusters. Photograph leaves and flowers together; several cultivated coral trees share similar features.
actions: Note whether the tree is planted or growing wild. Ask a local botanist or extension office to identify unexpected seedlings before deciding on management.
researchNotes: RHS supplies horticultural morphology; Kew supplies native and introduced ranges. The draft does not extrapolate invasive impacts from ornamental cultivation or introduced status alone.

claims: Prickly branches, three leaflets, scarlet flowers and ornamental habit.
South American native range and introductions.

proposedDescription: Taro is the plant behind a familiar tropical food crop and many garden elephant ears. Its large, heart- to arrow-shaped leaves rise from a thick underground corm. In warm wetlands, escaped plants can spread into dense patches along streams, ditches, and marshes, shading smaller vegetation. Pieces of the underground plant can help establish new patches when moved. Its value in cultivation and its ability to invade some waterways are both part of the story; the local setting matters.
identification: The leaf stalk attaches to the underside of the blade, inward from its edge. Photograph that attachment and the whole plant to distinguish similar elephant ears.
actions: Keep garden waste out of waterways. Wear gloves during removal and collect underground pieces; consult local wetland managers for established patches. Do not eat raw plant material.
researchNotes: NC State documents food and ornamental use and raw-plant irritation; UF documents Florida wetland escape and vegetative spread. Cultivation is not treated as proof of harm at every recorded location.

claims: Wetland stands, shading, underground fragments and removal precautions.
Corm-forming food and ornamental crop, large leaves and raw-plant hazards.

proposedDescription: Coconut palms are a familiar part of tropical coastlines, with a ringed trunk, long feather-like fronds, and large fibrous fruits. People have carried them widely for food, fiber, and useful materials. They also grow outside cultivation in suitable coastal habitats, where their ecological role depends on the place. Florida's assessment, for example, treats the palm differently across the state and identifies invasive behavior in the south with limited approved uses. A coconut record therefore needs more context than a garden label.
identification: Look for a single ringed trunk, a crown of long divided fronds, and large husked fruits. Young palms may still have the attached germinating nut.
actions: Before planting near natural shorelines, check local guidance. Record whether a palm is planted or self-established; have a qualified professional handle removal of large palms.
researchNotes: NParks provides morphology and uses; UF's regional assessment supports the Florida distinction. The draft avoids a definitive ancestral origin because long cultivation complicates that history.

claims: Palm morphology, fruit structure, coastal cultivation and uses.
South Florida invasive with limited approved uses; caution in central Florida; undocumented problem status in north Florida.

proposedDescription: Coconut scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that can gather in pale, closely packed patches on leaves. Coconut and banana are familiar hosts, but it also feeds on many other tropical crops and ornamental plants. Heavy infestations yellow and weaken foliage. Young insects, called crawlers, move before settling beneath a protective covering; infested nursery plants can carry them to new places. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps help suppress populations, so visible scales do not automatically mean broad insecticide treatment is needed.
identification: Look beneath leaves for small, flat, translucent covers with yellowish centers and nearby yellowing. Confirmation requires a specialist examining adult females under a microscope.
actions: Keep suspect plants from being moved or shared. Send clear photographs to extension or a plant clinic, and seek treatment advice that protects beneficial insects.
researchNotes: UF supplies diagnostic limitations and its own observations; Hawaii extension supplies host damage and natural-enemy management. Old pesticide lists and conflicting reproduction claims are excluded.

claims: Armored covering, crawler stage, host distribution and microscopic identification requirement.
Leaf yellowing, nursery movement and beneficial-insect suppression.

proposedDescription: Codling moth is best known for the caterpillar that tunnels into an apple or pear and feeds around the seeds. Adults are small, mottled moths that blend into bark; the damage inside fruit is usually more noticeable than the moth itself. It also attacks walnuts and some other fruit crops. Several generations can develop during a growing season, depending on climate. Successful management combines watching for moth activity with timely fruit protection and removing infested fruit before more insects emerge.
identification: Adults have a coppery patch near each forewing tip. Larvae become pale pink with a brown head; entry holes may have crumbly brown waste around them.
actions: Collect infested and fallen fruit promptly. Ask local extension about monitoring traps, fruit bagging, and seasonal management; timing varies with local weather and orchard conditions.
researchNotes: UC and Utah State independently cover orchard biology and management. Generation counts and treatment schedules are not generalized nationwide, and no pesticide rates are prescribed.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Codling moth
Utah State Extension: Codling moth in Utah orchards

claims: Fruit hosts, tunneling damage and home-orchard management.
Copper-tipped adult wings, pink larvae, frass, monitoring and sanitation.

proposedDescription: Hairy willow-herb is a tall perennial with fuzzy stems and pink-purple flowers, often growing where the soil stays moist. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form dense patches along wetlands, ditches, and stream edges in North America. Underground stems help a patch expand, while silky-haired seeds travel on the wind. Its flowers can be attractive, but a crowded stand can leave less room for other wetland plants. Native willow-herbs and fireweeds make careful identification worthwhile before any removal.
identification: Look for hairy stems, opposite toothed leaves, four notched pink petals, and a pale four-part stigma. Photograph the flowers and leaf arrangement to separate lookalikes.
actions: For a confirmed small patch, seek permission and local advice before digging, remove underground growth, and prevent seed release. Avoid disturbing sensitive wetland vegetation.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supplies identification and control; Native Plant Trust independently describes regional ecology and morphology. No legal status or nationwide abundance is inferred from occurrence records.

claims: Rhizomes, seeds, diagnostic flowers and patch management.
Eurasian origin, dense wetland stands and opposite toothed leaves.

proposedDescription: Cogongrass is a spreading perennial grass that can turn varied vegetation into dense stands. Its extensive underground stems help it survive disturbance and move outward, while fluffy seeds and contaminated soil or equipment carry it farther. In the southeastern United States, it invades roadsides, pastures, and natural areas. The buildup of dry grass also increases fire danger and can change how habitats burn. Because a patch can regrow from underground pieces, controlling it usually takes a coordinated effort and repeated follow-up.
identification: Look for upright blades with a pale midrib noticeably off center and silvery, fluffy seed heads. Other grasses resemble it; have a specialist confirm suspected patches.
actions: Avoid mowing seed heads or moving soil from the patch. Clean equipment and contact local extension or land managers. Burning alone is not a solution.
researchNotes: UF and Mississippi State support identification, rhizome spread, fire effects and persistent management. The draft avoids chemical prescriptions and treats large infestations as a professional planning task.

sources.title: Mississippi State Extension: Cogongrass identification and control

claims: Off-center midrib, dense rhizomes, equipment spread and fire effects.
Persistence after disturbance, fire concerns and repeated control.

proposedDescription: Colocynth, sometimes called bitter apple, is a trailing relative of watermelon adapted to dry landscapes. Its rough, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flowers spread close to the ground, followed by round fruits that change from mottled green to yellow. Unlike a sweet watermelon, the fruit has intensely bitter flesh. The plant is native across parts of Africa and Asia and adjacent regions. Its desert ecology is well documented, but a record outside that range does not alone establish local invasive damage.
identification: Look for a sprawling vine with deeply lobed leaves, tendrils, yellow flowers, and small round yellowing melons. Do not use tasting as an identification test.
actions: Photograph leaves, flowers, and fruit, and ask a botanist to confirm unexpected plants. Keep unidentified melons out of food and avoid spreading their seeds.
researchNotes: Kew's regional floras support detailed morphology; Flora of Israel independently supports desert habitat. The draft does not claim documented U.S. ecological impacts or offer medicinal or food uses.

sources.title: Kew: Citrullus colocynthis, regional flora descriptions

claims: Trailing perennial, lobed leaves, yellow flowers, bitter yellowing fruit and range.
Independent desert habitat and perennial life-form account.

proposedDescription: Colombian waxweed is a small, branching herb with rough, hairy leaves and tiny purple to pink flowers. It can be easy to overlook among grasses in a damp, disturbed patch. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has become established in other warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. The flower's narrow tube and the plant's sticky hairs help distinguish it from superficially similar weeds. Its introduced presence alone does not tell us how strongly it affects a particular habitat.
identification: Look for a low, branching, hairy plant with small oval leaves and tiny purple flowers emerging from narrow tubes. A close photograph is more useful than a distant patch view.
actions: Have unfamiliar plants identified before removal. Where management is warranted, address small patches before seed develops and avoid moving seed-bearing material into nearby natural areas.
researchNotes: Kew supports range; the independent Flora Malesiana treatment supplies morphology. The draft does not infer serious U.S. ecological impacts from naturalized status.

claims: Native tropical-American and introduced ranges.
Branched glandular-hairy herb, small rough leaves, tubular purple/red flowers.

proposedDescription: Colonial bentgrass, also called Rhode Island bentgrass, is a fine-leaved perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. Its airy flower clusters can give an unmown patch a soft haze. It has long been used in lawns, but also grows in fields, roadsides, and other open ground beyond cultivation. In some regions it becomes an invasive grass rather than staying a lawn plant. Separating it from related bentgrasses takes a closer look at the flowering branches and the small membranous flap where a leaf blade meets its sheath.
identification: Look for narrow leaves and a loose, branching flower cluster. The short membranous flap (ligule) at the blade-sheath junction helps distinguish it from creeping bentgrass and redtop.
actions: Keep lawn seed and soil from spreading into nearby natural grasslands. Ask a grass specialist to confirm suspect wild patches before choosing a restoration approach.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust supplies regional ecology and diagnostic comparisons; Kew independently supports native range and perennial habit. The common name does not indicate North American nativity.

claims: Introduced lawn grass, open habitats and short ligule diagnostic.
Native Eurasian range and perennial grass habit.

proposedDescription: This colonial sea squirt forms thin living sheets over surfaces such as dock structures, ropes, rocks, and shellfish. Each sheet contains many tiny animals that filter food from the water. Colonies often look pale or marbled, but their appearance changes with conditions. It has spread through warm-water ports and can overgrow other organisms, creating concerns for aquaculture and some natural habitats. Its original home remains uncertain in parts of the scientific literature, even though introductions are documented in several regions.
identification: A thin, pale encrusting colony may be a clue, but color cannot confirm the species. Specialists examine microscopic structures and sometimes use genetic evidence.
actions: Photograph suspect growth and report it to local marine biosecurity staff. Follow approved hull and gear cleaning practices; avoid scraping live fouling into the water.
researchNotes: Smithsonian treats much of the range as cryptogenic; NIMPIS labels Caribbean origin. Draft retains uncertainty and uses NIMPIS's regional observations and explicit identification caution, without claiming all U.S. records are equally secure.

claims: Colonial filter feeder, uncertain origin, fouling habitat and overgrowth impacts.
Independent Australian monitoring, variable appearance and aquaculture fouling.

proposedDescription: Symplegma reptans is a colonial sea squirt that spreads as a low covering of many small animals joined within a shared outer layer. Native to the Indo-West Pacific, it has established in Southern California harbors, where it grows on docks, hulls, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies expand by producing new individuals through budding. At some sites they can cover large areas and compete for space with other attached organisms. Its resemblance to related sea squirts has complicated identification and some early records.
identification: Look for flattened individuals visible within a thin, nearly transparent colony. Species-level identification requires a tunicate specialist; photographs alone may not separate related Symplegma.
actions: Record the location and photograph the colony. Ask local marine specialists about identification and follow marina guidance for cleaning fouled equipment without releasing living material.
researchNotes: Smithsonian supports invasion history and resemblance to congeners. Independent developmental research supports budding; only its accessible abstract was used, not unseen full-text claims.

sources.title: Kawamura and Nakauchi: Development of buds in Symplegma reptans

claims: Indo-West Pacific origin, Southern California introduction, fouling habitat and identification history.
Direct observations show colony members develop through budding.

proposedDescription: Coltsfoot sends up yellow, dandelion-like flower heads before its broad leaves unfold. Later, the leaves form a low cover, with a pale, woolly underside that helps distinguish them from dandelions. Native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa, this perennial grows in moist disturbed ground and can spread into nearby habitats. Underground stems allow it to form persistent patches, while its fluffy seeds provide another route of dispersal. Removing only the visible leaves often leaves the living network below intact.
identification: Look for early yellow flowers on short, scaly or woolly stalks, followed by broad heart-shaped leaves with white-felted undersides. Dandelion leaves are differently shaped.
actions: For confirmed small patches, remove underground growth before seed spreads and monitor regrowth. Ask local land managers about established patches, particularly near wetlands.
researchNotes: Kew independently supports native range; Wisconsin DNR supports identification, spread and management. Outdated chemical recommendations in the source are deliberately excluded.

claims: Flowers before leaves, woolly leaf undersides, rhizome persistence and removal guidance.
Eurasian and North African native range and perennial habit.

proposedDescription: Comb bushmint is a branching, aromatic herb whose tiny pale flowers line curved clusters like the teeth of a comb. It can grow tall enough to look like a small shrub, with toothed, hairy leaves and angular stems. Native to tropical America, it now occurs in other warm regions, often around disturbed ground, thickets, and moist edges. Although it appears in weed records, Florida's assessment does not document it as a problem species there. Its local behavior deserves attention without assuming severe impacts everywhere.
identification: Look for toothed, hairy leaves and branching clusters of small whitish to pale mauve flowers arranged along one side. Confirm against other bushmints.
actions: Photograph flowering branches and the whole plant. If it is spreading into a managed habitat, seek identification and local guidance before deciding whether control is needed.
researchNotes: Hyptis pectinata is now Mesosphaerum pectinatum in Kew and UF. Kew provides regional-flora morphology; UF independently provides a bounded Florida assessment. Queue identifier remains unchanged.

sources.title: Kew: Mesosphaerum pectinatum, regional flora descriptions

claims: Comb-like inflorescences, aromatic herb, toothed hairy leaves and habitat.
Florida problem status undocumented; synonym and growth form.

proposedDescription: Rangoon creeper is a woody climber best known for fragrant flowers that change from white through pink to red as they age. Hooks formed from leaf stalks help it climb over supports, and its broad leaves grow in opposite pairs. Its native range includes Tanzania and tropical and subtropical Asia through northern Australia. Widely cultivated in tropical gardens, it has also been introduced elsewhere. The mix of flower colors on a single vine makes it especially distinctive when in bloom.
identification: Look for opposite oval leaves, hooked climbing structures, and clusters containing differently aged white, pink, and red flowers. Quisqualis indica is an older name.
actions: Record whether the vine is cultivated or spreading outside a garden. Contain prunings and ask local extension about management of confirmed escapes.
researchNotes: NParks supports floral changes and climbing morphology; Kew supports accepted name, broader native range and introductions. No unsupported blanket U.S. invasion impact is asserted.

claims: Flower color changes, woody climbing habit, hooks and opposite leaves.
Native and introduced ranges; Quisqualis indica synonym.

proposedDescription: Common asparagus-fern looks soft and fern-like, but it is a flowering climber rather than a true fern. Its fine green sprays are familiar in houseplants and floral arrangements. Outside cultivation in warm regions, thorny shoots can climb through other vegetation, and birds carry seeds from its dark berries. Persistent underground growth makes established plants difficult to remove completely. Native to eastern and southern Africa, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere; Florida guidance recommends preventing escape and managing existing plants carefully.
identification: Look for fine, feathery sprays on wiry climbing stems, small flowers, and berries that ripen dark. Check for thorns and distinguish it from other ornamental asparagus species.
actions: Wear gloves, prevent berries from scattering, and remove the crown and underground growth where appropriate. Recheck for regrowth and keep discarded plants out of natural areas.
researchNotes: UF documents escape and practical control; Kew independently supports native and introduced ranges. The draft identifies it as a flowering plant and avoids treating all asparagus-ferns as one species.

claims: Climbing habit, dark bird-dispersed berries, persistent roots and removal precautions.
Eastern and southern African origin and introduced distribution.

proposedDescription: Lemon balm is a perennial herb with wrinkled, toothed leaves that release a lemon scent when bruised. A member of the mint family, it produces small pale flowers visited by pollinators and has long been grown for kitchen and garden use. Native from the Mediterranean toward Central Asia, it has become established well beyond that range. Plants can spread and self-seed around gardens, so keeping an eye on seedlings is useful. Its familiar usefulness and occasional weedy behavior are both worth recognizing.
identification: Look for opposite, wrinkled oval leaves, square stems, and small pale two-lipped flowers. Scent can support identification but should not replace checking the plant's features.
actions: Remove unwanted seedlings and trim flowers before seed forms if spread is a concern. Keep garden waste contained and confirm identification before using any wild herb.
researchNotes: NC State provides morphology, garden uses and spread management; Kew independently supports range. The draft avoids medicinal promises or assuming serious ecosystem damage from naturalization alone.

claims: Lemon-scented leaves, flowers, garden use, self-seeding and spread.
Mediterranean to Central Asian origin and widespread introductions.

proposedDescription: Common bamboo forms large clumps of tall, jointed canes topped by leafy branches. Native to parts of Asia and widely planted in warm regions, it supplies material for buildings, tools, and crafts as well as garden screens. It is a clumping bamboo, so its growth differs from the long-running bamboos familiar in some gardens. That distinction matters when evaluating a sighting or planning management. Florida's completed assessment for its southern region does not document an invasive problem there; other regions need their own assessment.
identification: Look for a dense clump of substantial jointed canes and narrow, pointed leaves. Cane colors vary among cultivars; a bamboo specialist may need sheath and branching details.
actions: Record whether the clump is planted and whether it is expanding beyond its intended area. Seek experienced help with large canes, and contain discarded rhizome pieces.
researchNotes: NParks supports habit, morphology and uses; UF independently distinguishes regional assessment status, including incomplete northern and central assessments. This is not Phyllostachys aurea, also called golden bamboo.

claims: Large clumping bamboo, jointed canes, narrow leaves and material uses.
Regional assessment results and incomplete-assessment distinctions.
